Ledger of Small Debts

Chapter 4: The Weighing Room

The weighing room had been built for grain and never quite forgave the clerks for filling it with paper instead, so it kept the smell of husks in the beams and let it down over the desks on warm afternoons.

Anselm arrived early because arriving early was the only part of the work he was reliably good at, and because the window seat went to whoever wanted it enough to be cold for an hour.

The ledgers were stacked by year, then by district, then by whatever principle the previous clerk had believed in before he stopped coming, and nobody had been brave enough to ask what that principle was.

"You are in my chair," said Mirren, who was not early and did not intend to become the sort of person who was.

He moved. It cost him nothing and bought him a morning without an argument, which by the standards of the weighing room was an excellent rate of exchange.

By noon the entry he had been looking for since spring turned up in the wrong district under the wrong year, written in a hand he recognised and signed with a name that had no business being there at all.

He copied it twice, put one copy in his coat, and went on weighing paper until the light failed and the clerks went home.
